clue.text: This marine organism has first to be dealt with

indicators.note: cards that are dealt get shuffled first, so these letters are to be mixed up

explanation.surface: A creature of the sea is told it has to go to the front of the queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be dealt with' shuffles the letters of HAS FIRST.
explanation.definitionFit: A starfish is an echinoderm living on the sea bed, a sea creature.

clue.text: Good man — regular guy

parts.note: ST, for saint, is the crossword's good man
even means regular, steady

explanation.surface: Someone vouches for an ordinary, decent bloke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular guy' reads as one phrase, but 'guy' alone is the definition, a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Steven is a common man's first name, and a guy is any man.

clue.text: Setting a worker on edge in Northern Ireland

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece placed on another comes above it, so first

parts.note: a worker ant is a member of an ant colony
a rim is the edge of something round

explanation.surface: A scene in Belfast where an employee is made nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setting' reads as the definition but only tells you to place the pieces; ANTRIM is a county of Northern Ireland, defined by where it lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is a county and town located in the north-east of Ulster.

clue.text: Better impose a penalty, right?

parts.note: to fine someone is to impose a penalty

explanation.surface: A referee wonders whether penalising a player is the correct thing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Finer means of higher quality, superior.

clue.text: Firm stem

explanation.surface: A two-word description of a sturdy plant stalk.
explanation.definitionFit: Staunch means loyal and steadfast; to staunch blood is to stop its flow.

clue.text: Reverse? That's in green

parts.note: vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether turning something round counts as an eco-friendly act.
explanation.walkthrough: VERT is green in heraldry, the language of coats of arms.
explanation.definitionFit: To invert something is to turn it upside down or back to front.

clue.text: This is not material for a composer, but it is for a writer

definitions.text: This is not material for a composer, but it is for a writer

parts.words: This is not material for a composer, but it is for a writer
parts.note: a composer writes music on staved manuscript, but someone writing letters uses ordinary plain sheets, though the name suggests music

explanation.surface: Something unsuitable for a musician but suited to an author.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that the item's name contains a musical 'note', yet it is no use for writing music.
explanation.definitionFit: Notepaper is stationery used for writing letters.

clue.text: A man with will-power

parts.note: will here is a legal testament, and the person named in it holds the power to carry it out

explanation.surface: A strong-minded man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will-power' suggests determination, but means authority under a will.
explanation.definitionFit: An executor is the person appointed to carry out the terms of a dead person's will.

clue.text: Take off underwear — put in a carrier

indicators.note: put in tells us one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a tray carries plates and cups
a vest is an undergarment in British English

explanation.surface: Someone strips off a garment and places it in a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests undressing but means mimic; a VEST in Britain is a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a mocking imitation, a parody of something serious.

clue.text: North European school-head taken in by a schoolboy

indicators.note: something taken in by another is held inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: an Etonian is a pupil at Eton College

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, here of the word school

explanation.surface: A headmaster from northern Europe is fooled by one of his pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school-head' gives S, the first letter of school; ETONIAN is a boy at Eton, the famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: An Estonian comes from Estonia, a Baltic country in northern Europe.

clue.text: Articles about next divine female

parts.note: a, the and an are the articles of English grammar
a, the and an are the articles of English grammar

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word an is read backwards

parts.note: a, the and an are the articles of English grammar

explanation.surface: A magazine's pieces concern the next goddess to be covered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' supplies three words, A, THE and AN; 'about' turns AN into NA, and 'next' just places it after the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom, a female deity.

clue.text: A once-revered figure, as is written repeatedly

indicators.note: written repeatedly means the word is is set down twice in a row

explanation.surface: A statue that used to be worshipped is described again and again.
explanation.definitionFit: Isis was an ancient Egyptian goddess, worshipped in antiquity.

clue.text: People getting out-streaming out

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters of streaming are rearranged

explanation.surface: Crowds pour out of a place in a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'out' is the anagram signal for STREAMING.
explanation.definitionFit: Emigrants are people leaving their own country to settle abroad.

clue.text: Cut pieces off dried fruit

explanation.surface: Someone trims bits from a piece of dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To prune is to trim off branches; a prune is also a dried plum.

clue.text: Some appear churlish, some sly

indicators.note: some here means only part of the following words, so the letters sit inside them

explanation.surface: A remark that certain people seem rude and others crafty.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'appear' and the start of 'churlish'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch describes a knowing, mischievous manner, as in an arch smile.

clue.text: A footballer it's OK to patronise!

parts.note: OK means all right, correct
to patronise a business is to support or back it

explanation.surface: A soccer player whom one may talk down to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patronise' suggests condescension but here means support.
explanation.definitionFit: A right back is a defender playing on the right side of a team.

clue.text: Back up in play

indicators.note: in signals that one word sits inside another

parts.note: sport is play, games for fun
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is reinforcing a structure during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back up' looks like one phrasal verb, but only 'Back' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a cause or person is to give them help and encouragement.

clue.text: Disturbances causing tears in the main?

definitions.text: Disturbances causing tears in the main?

parts.words: Disturbances causing tears in the main?
parts.note: tears read as rips rather than weeping, and the main is the open sea, so these are currents tearing through it

explanation.surface: Upsets that mostly make people cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is an old word for the sea; 'tears' rhymes with bears, not beers.
explanation.definitionFit: Riptides are strong currents pulling against the tide, turbulent water.

clue.text: He rates the fools bearing EL with an alternative

parts.note: asses are fools
S, south, is a compass bearing
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A man judges the idiots holding a different view.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints a stray 'EL' after 'bearing', an OCR error to be ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor values property for rates and taxes.

clue.text: A discerning gift in a sense

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses

explanation.surface: A present that shows great taste, wrapped in a feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Insight is a talent for perceiving the true nature of things.

clue.text: Running water can be such NI a trial!

explanation.surface: Flowing water may be an ordeal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Test is a chalk-stream river in Hampshire, England; the page also prints a stray 'NI'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Test is an English river, flowing water; a test is also a trial.

clue.text: Battle involving a hundred soldiers

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: An account of an engagement fought by a company of a hundred men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' is a link here: the pieces simply follow one another.
explanation.definitionFit: The siege of Acre in 1189-91 was a famous Crusade battle in Palestine.

clue.text: A crime changing a large Ex part of the Western world At

indicators.note: changing means the letters of a crime are put in a new order

explanation.surface: An offence reshapes much of the West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing' rearranges A CRIME; 'large' only colours the surface, and the stray 'Ex' and 'At' on the page are OCR noise.
explanation.definitionFit: America covers a vast area of the western hemisphere.

clue.text: 22 A sea-monster turning 32 co ocean-going craft over

indicators.note: turning means the word for the sea-monster is read backwards

parts.note: an orc is a mythical sea-monster, or a killer whale
SS, steamship, prefixes the names of ocean liners

explanation.surface: A sea-beast capsizes a liner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses ORC to CRO; the stray '22' and '32 co' on the page are OCR noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Across means from one side to the other, as in over the road.

clue.text: An old Jew having a little less energy these days

indicators.note: having a little of the next words means taking letters held within them

explanation.surface: An elderly Jewish man feels less lively nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'less energy'; 'these days' completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The Essenes were an ascetic Jewish sect of Roman times.

clue.text: Free entertainment makes the heartless sailor scoff

indicators.note: heartless means the middle letter of the word for sailor is removed

parts.note: tar is a traditional word for a sailor
to scoff is to eat greedily

explanation.surface: A cruel seaman wolfs down food at a free show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' takes the middle A from TAR, leaving TR.
explanation.definitionFit: A treat is something paid for by someone else, an outing or meal given free.

clue.text: The woman with money avoids wildfowl

parts.note: she refers to a woman
L stands for pound, from Latin libra
to duck something is to dodge it

explanation.surface: A wealthy woman sidesteps her responsibilities, or a flock of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelducks are large Old World waterbirds, a kind of wild duck.

clue.text: Getting a large number back is dismal

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred, a large number
the rear is the back

explanation.surface: Being paid a lot again is depressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a reversal signal, but it is REAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic word for gloomy and cheerless.

clue.text: Give the underworld boss a month and there's consternation!

parts.note: Dis was the Roman god ruling the realm of the dead
May is a month of the year

explanation.surface: Someone grants a crime lord thirty-one days and everyone is alarmed.
explanation.walkthrough: DIS, also called Pluto, was the Roman ruler of the dead, not a gangster.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay is a feeling of distress and alarm at something unexpected.

clue.text: Boring ties — more variety is needed

indicators.note: a call for variety asks for the letters of ties and more to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that neckwear is dull and a wider range should be stocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety is needed' rearranges TIES and MORE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiresome means tedious, wearying through dullness.

clue.text: All out to impress

explanation.surface: Workers all down tools to make a point.
explanation.definitionFit: A strike is when all workers walk out; to strike also means to make an impression on someone.

clue.text: A sport left a snappy note

parts.note: snappy can mean irritable, as is cross
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: A player departs leaving a short, sharp message behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snappy' here means bad-tempered, not quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team game played with netted sticks and a ball.
